newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish govt spending growing too fast - analysts.
newsitem.headline: Irish govt spending growing too fast - analysts.

text.p: Irish government expenditure is growing too fast and could lead to trouble in the future if the strong Irish economic growth seen in recent years tails off, analysts said.
The Irish government published its 1997 spending estimates on Monday and breached its own self-imposed targets for the second year in a row.
Finance Minister Ruairi Quinn announced that gross current spending after the 1997 budget would be capped at 13 billion punts, a nominal increase of 6.1 percent on 1996 levels.
This represents a rise of 3.9 percent in real terms, well above the government's original two percent target.
"It's a disappointment from a financial market perspective. We don't really like it," one dealer said.
But analysts said the estimates were unlikely to upset Ireland's financial markets in the short-term given the government's commitment to maintaining a low general government deficit.

Quinn said on Monday that Ireland's general government deficit would be significantly lower than the 1996 target of 2.6 pct of GDP and comfortably within the Maastricht criteria for membership of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

"The market focus is not on spending. Provided nothing happens to prejudice the chance of a respectable deficit target being adopted in the budget, the market should show little interest," Jim O'Leary, chief economist at Davy Stockbrokers, told Reuters.
But analysts believe that the high level of current expenditure could cause trouble in the years ahead, particularly if Ireland's record economic growth slows.
The Irish economy has outperformed its EU neighbours in recent years with GNP growing at more than seven percent last year while growth of six percent is expected in 1996.
But analysts warn the good times cannot last for ever.

"There is a danger that when the economy slows down we will find ourselves in a difficult position, particularly if we have to live within the rigours of the EMU stability pact," Davy's O' Leary said.

Bank of Ireland economist Jim Power also believes that Ireland could fall foul of the proposed budget stability pact, aimed at ensuring fiscal discipline after the introduction of a single European currency.
"There is an assumption underlying the estimates that the economy will continue to grow strongly. That is a very dangerous assumption to make."
"Once the economy turns down here, we are very exposed and Ireland could be a victim of the stability pact three or four years down the road," Power said.

But strong economic growth should again come to the government's rescue in the near-term, analysts said, allowing it to introduce significant tax reform in its January budget despite the big increase in spending planned for 1997.

Analysts expect tax cuts totalling more than 250 million Irish pounds from the budget while the government is expected to target a general government deficit of 2.0 pct of GDP or less in 1997. -- Dublin Newsroom +353 1 676 9779
